name: Rembarnga
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: McKay, Graham Richard. 1975. Rembarnga: a language of central Arnhem Land. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. xvii+406 pp. Open access:https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/handle/1885/11030(republished 2011, München: LINCOM Europa, ISBN 9783862880898).

catalog_quote: In the present brief discussion I give an outline of the use of stress in Rembarnga only at the level of words and make no attempt to deal with sentence patterns of stress. ... in slow speech more stresses will be present than in fast speech where only the main stresses (i.e. the first stress in the root and/or the first stress in the word) are present. Word stress in Rembarnga is very largely predictable on the basis of word and morpheme boundaries, but not entirely. Put another way, we can say that each morpheme has its own particular stress pattern but that stress on a vast majority of morphemes follows a certain small number of patterns definable in terms of word and morpheme boundaries. The principal pattern involved is one of morpheme initial stress and in particular of primary stress on the first syllable of the root (in complex verbal and nominal forms). Two other patterns are also important: stress on alternate syllables, and antepenultimate (word) stress. ... 1.6.1 Root Stress. For all major word classes the vast majority of roots have stress on the first syllable. ... Some roots have their first stress on syllables other than the first. ... 1.6.2 Prefix Stress ... In general monosyllabic prefixes have no stress at all while di- and polysyllabic prefixes have morpheme initial stress. ... 1.6.3 Suffix Stress. In general monosyllabic suffixes bear no stress (but see (i) below) while di- and polysyllabic suffixes bear morpheme initial stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root, whatever prefixes precede it (morpheme-initial stress); p. 57: 'For all major word classes the vast majority of roots have stress on the first syllable.' In a bare disyllabic or trisyllabic root this is word-initial stress. Longer roots and polysyllabic affixes carry further stresses on alternate syllables (4-syllable roots: 1st and 3rd; 5-syllable: mostly 1st and 3rd = antepenult), and a third pattern, antepenultimate word stress, arises in derived forms and before the future suffix -ŋara. Monosyllabic prefixes and suffixes are normally unstressed; polysyllabic ones take morpheme-initial stress. Stress is described as 'potential for being stressed' (after Lehiste): in fast speech only the main stresses (first stress in the root and/or first in the word) surface.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'stress on alternate syllables' — 4-syllable roots stressed on 1st and 3rd (e.g. 'perer?'perer? 'bird type'); prefixes 'potentially stressed every alternate syllable forward towards word initial position', but each such stress must be morpheme-initial and counting restarts from the last allotted stress (p. 62); reduplicated polysyllabic roots repeat the root stress on each copy; monosyllabic reduplicants stress only the first copy (p. 61). In long prefix strings (4-8 syllables) normally at least the stress nearest word-initial position is realised.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical residue: 1 noun and 10 verbs of two syllables stressed on the 2nd syllable (pe'rer, ka'pur? 'bury'); 1 verb + 6 nouns of three syllables with 2nd-syllable stress (ka'taykka 'stringy bark'); a few 4-syllable roots with initial+final stress, 5 reduplicated roots stressed on 2nd and 4th, one root with 2nd-syllable-only (antepenult) stress; some roots vary ('meren?/me'ren?). Morphophonological shifts: if root+suffix form one syllable and the prefix is monosyllabic, stress shifts to the prefix ('par-ŋur < par'ŋur); a lengthened monosyllabic past suffix marking duration takes stress and a monosyllabic stem loses its stress; future -ŋara (conj. 5) places stress on the immediately preceding syllable (antepenult), the root-initial syllable then losing its stress (possibly moving to a monosyllabic prefix); a monosyllabic suffix may shift stress of a disyllabic root to root-final/penult ('tiyalŋ but ti'yalŋ-na ~ 'tiyalŋna).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level explicitly: 'an outline of the use of stress in Rembarnga only at the level of words and make no attempt to deal with sentence patterns of stress' (p. 57). Word = polysynthetic verbal/nominal complex (prefixes + root + suffixes); the primary stress is anchored to the root, not to the word edge, so in prefixed words it is word-medial. Based on the author's fieldwork (1972-75); auditory, not instrumental.
new_statements.identity_note: McKay 1975 describes Rembarnga as spoken at Bamyili (Barunga) and Maningrida area, central Arnhem Land, from the author's own 1972-75 fieldwork; this is the language-level variety remb1249 (spelling 'Rembarnga' = Rembarrnga). No dialect split is given in the stress section.
